questions.q: Why is a "stalled" training run harder to catch than a crashed one?
options: Stalled runs always consume more GPU memory
The job still reports Running and pods are alive, so no discrete failure event fires an obvious alert
Stalled runs cannot be detected by any monitoring tool
Stalled runs always resolve themselves within a minute
questions.explain: A crash produces a clear status change to Failed. A stall looks healthy at a glance — process alive, pods Running — so it requires watching a trend over time rather than a single discrete event.

questions.q: What does the PromQL expression `changes(solara_training_loss{namespace="training-lm"}[30m]) == 0` detect?
options: That the loss has decreased by more than 30% in 30 minutes
That the loss metric's value has not changed at all over the last 30 minutes
That the job has been running for exactly 30 minutes
That GPU utilization is exactly zero
questions.explain: changes() counts how many times a metric's value changed over the given window; a result of zero means the value has been frozen, a sign training progress has stopped.

questions.q: Why does the Alertmanager rule in this lesson use `for: 15m` instead of firing immediately when GPU utilization drops under 5%?
options: Prometheus requires all rules to wait exactly 15 minutes
To avoid false positives from brief, normal dips, such as during checkpointing
Because GPU metrics are only updated every 15 minutes
15 minutes is the maximum alert duration Alertmanager supports
questions.explain: A sustained-duration requirement filters out short, legitimate dips (like a checkpoint save) that would otherwise trigger false alarms if the rule fired on an instantaneous reading.

questions.q: How does Alertmanager route a `TrainingJobStalled` alert to the correct research team?
options: By randomly assigning alerts to on-call engineers
By matching the alert's `namespace` label (training-lm or training-mm) to a routing rule with the corresponding receiver
All alerts are sent to every team regardless of namespace
By checking which team deployed Alertmanager
questions.explain: Because namespace is carried as a label on the alert, Alertmanager's route configuration can match on it and send the alert to that team's specific receiver, such as a Slack channel.

questions.q: Why does the lesson recommend combining a GPU-utilization signal with a loss-metric signal to detect a stall, rather than relying on just one?
options: Because Prometheus requires at least two conditions per alert rule
Because neither signal alone is perfect — each can have legitimate, non-stall explanations for a brief anomaly
Because loss metrics are more accurate than GPU metrics in all cases
Because GPU metrics cannot be queried with PromQL
questions.explain: A brief GPU dip can be normal (e.g. during checkpointing) and a loss can plateau briefly for legitimate reasons, so using both signals together, each with a sustained-duration requirement, reduces false positives.
